description_full: Watts Water Technologies, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, supplies products and solutions that manage and conserve the flow of fluids and energy into, through, and out of buildings in the commercial, industrial, and residential markets. The company offers residential and commercial flow control and protection products, including backflow preventers, water pressure regulators, temperature and pressure relief valves, thermostatic mixing valves, leak detection and protection products, commercial washroom solutions, hydration solutions, and emergency safety products and equipment for plumbing and hot water applications. It also provides heating, ventilation, and air conditioning and gas products comprising commercial, institutional, and industrial boilers; water heaters and heating solutions; hydronic and electric heating systems for under-floor radiant applications; custom heat and hot water solutions; hydronic pump groups for boiler manufacturers and alternative energy control packages; and flexible stainless-steel connectors for natural and liquid propane gas in commercial food service and residential applications. In addition, the company offers drainage and water re-use products, such as drainage products, engineered rainwater harvesting solutions for commercial, industrial, marine, and residential applications; connected roof drain systems; and water quality products, including point-of-use and point-of-entry, closed loop, cooling tower, and other water applications for commercial, marine, and residential applications. It sells its products to plumbing, heating, and mechanical wholesale distributors and dealers; original equipment manufacturers; specialty product distributors; and do-it-yourself and retail chains, as well as wholesalers and private label accounts in the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Middle East, and Africa. Watts Water Technologies, Inc. was founded in 1874 and is headquartered in North Andover, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Watts Water Technologies, Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $11.9B market cap on $2.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 9% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 41%.

The business throws off $356M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.18× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 41× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.7%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 33% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $7.8M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 9% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
35 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 9pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.64x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+6.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 32% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 27% and a beta of 0.93, it moves roughly with the market.
About $79.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 33% in the 2020 crash, 39% in the 2022 bear market and 50% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $267 (margin of safety -33%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $144 to $506 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: EV/EBITDA 18.8 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 33.4 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 60% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $393 on average, 10% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 9.1% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.66).
It runs a 41% gross margin and converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.18x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.0% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $207.8M (2% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 10.8, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 145 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.2% over 3 years, 10.1% over 5 years and 5.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 28% of profits supports about 5.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.0% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.8x, 1.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 24, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.9%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (14 sales, net $7.8M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.7% (0.1% in buybacks and 0.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 35 consecutive years.
people: With about 5,700 employees, each generates about $428K of revenue, 1.2x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 4.4% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $63K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.0M (9x revenue per employee).
